doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Piano lessons, Teddy Wilson in Hackensack and parents meeting musicians
summary: Early piano lessons, then seeing Teddy Wilson at a Hackensack restaurant; his parents befriend Wilson, Hank Jones and Eddie Durham and trust them as mentors.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Right. And John Thompson, “A Day in Bermuda” or whatever they called it. “A snowy Bird” you know, and learned all that stuff. And then, on this Benny Goodman record I listened to it and I looked at all the names and then in my local newspaper, the Bergen Evening Record I saw, I was about, I don’t know, 13 or 14, and it said, “Sundays at the Colonial Post on Main Street in Hackensack, New Jersey, Sundays maybe 5 PM to 8 PM Teddy Wilson.” And I said this cannot be the Teddy Wilson who’s on the Benny Goodman record I’m listening to at Carnegie Hall. I mean what would he be doing playing at an Italian restaurant in Hackensack, New Jersey? Well it turns out that Teddy lived in New Jersey as did Hank Jones, in Bergen County, and when he was around he took whatever gigs he could get just to keep his fingers in shape and maybe he was in between tours or whatever. And so my parents took me to see him and he was very kind and let me sit by the piano and look and all this kind of stuff. I mean I really had no inkling of what I was getting. I mean I knew he was great but all I knew was this one record and that I loved the music. And so my parents got to meet him. And that started a series of things where my parents would meet these musicians, now let’s put it in context. I mean these are African-American musicians. I’m a kid growing up in the 60s and 70s in Bergen County, New Jersey, which was one of the most un-diverse places there could be, although my town, called Fairlawn, was kind of unusual because it had a large Jewish population. On the day that my parents moved in in the 1950s to welcome the first Jewish family on the block everyone put up For Sale signs on all the houses, so they saw that as they drove up the first day. Then they took the signs down. So you know it was not a very diverse place. So what happened was my parents met Teddy Wilson and eventually met Hank Jones and eventually met Eddie Durham and a few other people who were so avuncular and so warm and supportive, my parents said we have no problem at all with our kid leaving him in these hands. Now if you had said to my parents your son’s going © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

to be a jazz musician and he’s going to be hanging out with these people with all the prejudices about, forget race for a moment, just about how jazz musicians are. I mean my parents were just normal, when I say normal people what I mean is they didn’t know anything about show biz or musicians.
He’s going to work in bars and live the night life.

Well, and all the negative connotations that again, due to race, that came to, you know as we find out that more, you know, physicians have problems with drugs than musicians, and that you know musicians are actually way down on the line. But anyway so you asked earlier about like when I knew I was going to be a musician — I think all these experiences kind of led to them. My parents saw like oh wow, there’s these wonderful mentors out there and they’re willing to answer Loren’s questions or something like that. And so that’s kind of part of the context.
